topics.title: 13.1 General-purpose registers
topics.summary: The baseline x86-64 general-purpose register set includes %rax , %rbx , %rcx , %rdx , %rsi , %rdi , %rsp , %rbp , and %r8 through %r15 . They can hold integer values or addresses, with some instructions imposing implicit operand roles. The ABI distinguishes caller-saved and callee-saved registers. Caller-saved values may be overwritten by a call, so a caller must preserve any such value it needs afterward. Callee-saved registers must be restored by a function that changes them. This division reduces unnecessary saving while allowing separately compiled functions to cooperate. [ R4 ]

topics.title: 13.2 Register widths
topics.summary: A 64-bit register has narrower named views. %rax is the full 64-bit register, %eax its low 32 bits, %ax its low 16 bits, and %al its low eight bits. %ah names another eight-bit portion, but legacy high-byte registers have encoding restrictions with REX prefixes and are best avoided in beginner examples. Writing a 32-bit general-purpose register zeroes the upper 32 bits of the corresponding 64-bit register. Writing a 16-bit or eight-bit subregister generally leaves the other bits unchanged. This is why movl $1, %eax establishes a full %rax value of one, while movb $1, %al does not.

topics.title: 13.3 %rax
topics.summary: %rax commonly carries an integer or pointer return value under the System V ABI. It is caller-saved. Some multiply and divide instructions use %rax implicitly, often together with %rdx for a double-width value. Do not assume a call preserves an unrelated value in %rax ; the callee is allowed to use it for the result and temporary work. The low byte %al also has a special role when calling variadic functions under this ABI: it conveys information about vector-register arguments. Handwritten assembly that calls a variadic library routine must follow that rule rather than only loading the visible integer arguments.

topics.title: 13.4 %rbx
topics.summary: %rbx is callee-saved in the reference calling convention. A function can use it for a long-lived local value across nested calls, but must restore the caller’s original value before returning. The cost of using %rbx may include a save and restore if the function changes it. A compiler weighs that cost against repeatedly saving a caller-saved value around calls. Register allocation is therefore influenced by value lifetimes and call structure, not simply by choosing the shortest register name.

topics.title: 13.5 %rcx
topics.summary: %rcx holds the fourth ordinary integer or pointer argument in the System V convention. It is caller-saved. The low byte %cl is also the implicit count operand for traditional variable-count shift instructions. Implicit roles can constrain instruction scheduling. A compiler may need to move a shift count into %cl even when the count originally resides elsewhere. In Linux’s x86-64 system-call ABI, the fourth argument is not passed in %rcx ; the syscall interface uses %r10 for that position. Function calls and system calls must be learned as separate interfaces.

topics.title: 13.9 %rsp
topics.summary: %rsp is the stack pointer. Push, pop, call, and return operations use it according to their instruction semantics. The ABI requires suitable alignment at call boundaries and restoration of the caller’s stack position before a normal return. Corrupting %rsp can redirect subsequent stack accesses and returns. Handwritten assembly must account for every push, pop, and explicit adjustment. A balanced count alone is not enough if the adjustments occur on only some control-flow paths. Trace the stack depth along every path to the return instruction.

topics.title: 13.10 %rbp
topics.summary: %rbp is callee-saved and can serve as a frame pointer. A conventional prologue saves the old value and makes %rbp a stable reference point for the current frame. Optimized code often omits this dedicated role and uses the register for other purposes. The absence of %rbp -based accesses does not mean a function lacks local state or cannot be unwound. Debugging and exception unwinding can use metadata that describes stack changes. Conversely, having a frame pointer does not make corrupted stack contents trustworthy.

topics.title: 13.11 %r8–%r15
topics.summary: %r8 and %r9 carry the fifth and sixth ordinary integer or pointer arguments. %r10 and %r11 are caller-saved temporaries. %r12 through %r15 are callee-saved. The narrower forms use suffixes such as %r8d , %r8w , and %r8b . These registers expand the available working set and reduce some memory spills compared with a smaller register set. They do not eliminate register pressure. Large expressions, vector work, and many simultaneously live values can still require spills to stack storage. A spill is a consequence of allocation constraints, not necessarily a sign of an incompetent compiler.

topics.title: 13.13 Condition flags
topics.summary: The flags register includes status bits such as zero, sign, carry, and overflow. Arithmetic and comparison instructions update selected flags. Conditional branches, conditional moves, and set-on-condition instructions then interpret them. Flags do not have one universal “comparison result” meaning. Signed and unsigned order use different combinations. Carry is relevant to unsigned overflow or borrow interpretation; overflow describes signed-range overflow for particular arithmetic operations. An intervening instruction can overwrite flags, so keep the producing instruction and consuming branch connected in the data-flow analysis. [ R3 ]

The flags register includes status bits such as zero, sign, carry, and overflow. Arithmetic and comparison instructions update selected flags.
